standard_prerequisites.name: Profiles of matchings in the hypercube
standard_prerequisites.statement: For a matching M in Q^n the profile is the vector x in N^n whose i-th coordinate counts the edges of M whose endpoints differ in the i-th coordinate; a tuple is admissible when it is the profile of some matching, even when every coordinate is even, and perfect when the sum of the coordinates equals 2^{n-1}; the article's own definitions are retained at source line 51.
standard_prerequisites.use: Fixes all objects of the counted lemma: admissible x, the perfect property of (2x, x_{n+1}) and the count 2||x||_1 + |X| = 2^n.

standard_prerequisites.name: Balister-Gyori-Schelp partitioning problem
standard_prerequisites.statement: Given d_1,...,d_{2^{n-1}} in the vector space over F_2 of dimension n, the sum of all d_i must vanish if the cube is to be partitioned into pairs with those differences; the article records this identity and the conjecture that it is also sufficient at source lines 30-36, and the case of unit-vector differences is the matching-profile problem.
standard_prerequisites.use: Background for why evenness is the necessary condition and why a perfect even profile is the interesting case; the counted lemma itself is used to build the inductive argument for that conjecture in the unit-vector case.

core_obligations: Start from a matching M_1 in Q^n with profile x, which exists by the admissibility hypothesis of the lemma.

Form the matching M_2 in Q^{n+1} as two disjoint copies of M_1, one in the slice with last coordinate 0 and one in the slice with last coordinate 1, and note that its profile is (2x, 0) (source lines 71-76).
Let X be the set of vertices of Q^n not covered by M_1 and compute |X| = 2^n - 2||x||_1, which is exactly the prescribed value of the new coordinate x_{n+1} (source line 78).

Add to M_2 the edges in direction e_{n+1} joining the two copies of every vertex of X, obtaining M_3, and verify that M_3 is still a matching and that its profile is (2x, x_{n+1}) (source lines 78-83).
Conclude that M_3 is perfect, because 2||x||_1 + |X| = 2^n, so that (2x, x_{n+1}) is a perfect admissible tuple (source line 83).

proof_roadmap.step: Take a matching M_1 in Q^n with profile x.
Build M_2 from two disjoint copies of M_1 and observe its profile (2x, 0).
Identify the uncovered vertex set X of Q^n and its size 2^n - 2||x||_1.
Add the e_{n+1} edges between the two copies of each vertex of X.
Check the profile and the perfection of M_3.

difficulty_reason: The counted unit is Lemma l:admissible at source lines 67-69: if x in N^n is an admissible profile and the new coordinate satisfies x_{n+1} = 2^n - 2||x||_1, then the concatenated tuple (2x, x_{n+1}) must be a perfect admissible tuple. The adjacent proof at source lines 70-84 has to construct the matching in the right ambient cube: it takes two disjoint copies of a matching M_1 with profile x inside Q^{n+1} (lines 71-76), then uses exactly the vertex set X of Q^n left uncovered by M_1, whose size is 2^n - 2||x||_1 = x_{n+1}, to add the direction-e_{n+1} edges joining the two copies of every uncovered vertex (lines 78-81). Both conclusions must then be checked, namely that M_3 is a matching with profile (2x, x_{n+1}) and that it is perfect because 2||x||_1 + |X| = 2^n (line 83). The step that is not a routine verification is the choice of the leftover set and the dimension, which makes the new coordinate absorb precisely the uncovered vertices; the argument is short and elementary once that choice is made, so it is rated H2.

compared.difference: Same source, different proposition: the counted public unit is Theorem t:perfect at source lines 53-55 with the long proof at 172-283, which characterises the perfect admissible tuples as the even ones. The present card counts Lemma l:admissible (source lines 67-69) with its own proof at 70-84, a sufficient condition producing one perfect admissible tuple from an admissible one; the public unit keeps the lemma's statement only as retained context (manifest context span 67-69) and does not retain its proof, and the lemma is a step towards the theorem rather than a corollary of it.
